learn.b: A dictionary stores data as key: value pairs inside curly braces. You look up a value by its key, not by a position. Keys must be unique and are usually strings or numbers.

learn.code:
d = {'a': 1}
print(d.get('z', 0))
print('a' in d)
print(1 in d)

learn.b: Looping over a dict gives its keys. Use .values() for values and .items() for both at once. items() gives key, value pairs you can unpack in the for line.

learn.b: A tuple is like a list but cannot be changed after it is made. It uses parentheses. A tuple with one item needs a trailing comma, like (5,). Tuples are great for fixed groups like coordinates.

learn.b: A set holds unique values with no order and no indexes. Making a set from a list removes duplicates. add() puts one in and remove() takes one out. An empty set must be set(), because {} is an empty dict.

learn.b: a | b is the union, a & b is what both share, and a - b is what is only in a. Sets are fast for checking membership. Use sorted(s) to see a set in a stable order.

learn.b: A list comprehension builds a new list in one line. The pattern is [expression for item in source]. It is a short way of writing a for loop that appends to a list.
learn.code:

learn.b: A variable created inside a function is local: it exists only while the function runs. Code outside cannot see it. Parameters are local too. This keeps functions from messing with each other.
learn.code:
def f():
    x = 5
    return x

print(f())
# print(x)  <- NameError

learn.b: A variable created outside all functions is global and can be read anywhere. Assigning to a name inside a function makes a new local variable instead. To change a global, declare it with the global keyword first. Prefer passing values and returning results.
learn.code:
count = 0
def bump():
    global count
    count += 1

bump()
bump()
print(count)

learn.b: Python looks for a name in this order: Local, Enclosing (functions around it), Global, then Built-in. This is called the LEGB rule. If two levels share a name, the closest one wins.
learn.code:
x = 'global'
def f():
    x = 'local'
    return x

print(f())
print(x)

learn.b: open(name, mode) gives you a file object. Modes: 'r' reads (the default), 'w' writes and erases what was there, 'a' adds to the end. Always close a file when finished, or better, use a with block that closes it for you.

f.write(text) writes exactly the text you give; it does not add a newline for you, so add \n yourself. Mode 'a' keeps old content and adds new text after it. f.writelines() writes a list of strings.
learn.code:

    f.write('new line\n')

learn.b: A class is a blueprint and an object is something built from it. For example, Dog is the class and your pet Rex is an object. You create an object by calling the class like a function.

learn.b: __init__ runs automatically when an object is created and sets it up. The first parameter is always self, which means this very object. Attributes are variables stored on the object with self.name.
A method is a function inside a class. It always takes self first so it can use the object's attributes. You call it with a dot: object.method(). Methods can change attributes or return values.

Every object has its own attributes, so changing one does not change another. A class attribute written directly in the class body is shared by all objects. Use clear names and keep one job per class.
learn.code:
class Dog:
    species = 'dog'
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

a = Dog('A')
b = Dog('B')
print(a.name, b.name, a.species)

learn.b: A child class can inherit everything from a parent class. Write the parent name in parentheses: class Dog(Animal). The child gets all the parent's methods for free and can add its own. Use it for is-a relationships: a Dog is an Animal.
A child can override a method by defining one with the same name. super() lets the child call the parent's version, which is common inside __init__. Python looks in the child first, then the parent.

Methods with double underscores on both sides, like __init__, are special methods Python calls for you. __str__ controls what print shows, __repr__ is the developer view, and __len__ is used by len().

__eq__ defines what == means for your objects and __add__ defines +. Without __eq__, two different objects are never equal even if their data matches. Dunder methods make your classes feel like built-in types.
